title: The road to Emmaus (Luke 24:13–35)
hookLine: two sad friends walk seven miles with a stranger and know him in the breaking of bread

cards: Same Sunday, late afternoon. Two of Jesus's followers are walking home from Jerusalem to a village called Emmaus, sixty furlongs away, Luke says, about seven miles. One is named Cleophas.
The other, Luke never names. They go over it again and again, the way people do on the long drive home from a funeral. A stranger falls into step beside them and asks what they're talking about.
They stop. Their faces fall. Are you the only visitor in Jerusalem who hasn't heard?
Then the words that give it all away: we had hoped he was the one. Had hoped. Past tense.

teach.b: The stranger is Jesus, but Luke says their eyes were held so they didn't know him. He doesn't reveal himself.
He walks with them and opens the Scriptures, from Moses through all the prophets, showing how the Messiah had to suffer and so enter his glory.

Seven miles of Bible study. At the village he acts as if he's going further, and they beg him, in the Douay-Rheims: "Stay with us, because it is towards evening, and the day is now far spent." He goes in.
At the table he takes the bread, blesses it, breaks it and gives it to them: the same four movements as the Last Supper. Their eyes are opened, they know him, and he vanishes.
They turn to each other: "Was not our heart burning within us, whilst he spoke in the way, and opened to us the scriptures?"
That same hour, Luke says, they walk the seven miles back, to tell the others how they knew him "in the breaking of bread." The Catechism sees the shape of the Mass in this road.
First the Word: the Scriptures read and opened.
Then the table: bread taken, blessed, broken, given.

teach.h: THE WORD, THEN THE TABLE: THE MASS.
teach.b: Two parts, in the order Luke tells it.

teach.h: WAS NOT OUR HEART BURNING WITHIN US?
teach.b: And notice where he's recognized. Not in the explaining, as good as it was. In the bread.
Pope John Paul II named a letter on the Eucharist after their plea: stay with us, Lord.

how: Catholics hear the Emmaus story in the Easter season, and the Catechism sees in it the two parts of every Mass: the Liturgy of the Word and the Liturgy of the Eucharist.

o: the town where Jesus was born
a village seven miles from Jerusalem
a mountain where Jesus prayed alone

games.q: what's inside the road — tap the pairs.
p: one of the two walking home
hope gone into the past tense

s: the two disciples recognized Jesus as soon as he joined them
Luke says their eyes were held. they knew him only at the table.
he names only Cleophas. the second is never named.
after he vanished, they walked back to Jerusalem that same night
that same hour, Luke says, to tell the others.

games.q: you've reached your village with a stranger who talked with you for seven miles. he acts as if he's going further. what do you do?
o: ask him to stay, since it's nearly evening.
games.why: "stay with us, because it is towards evening." he goes in, breaks the bread, and they know him.

practice: Bring to mind someone whose hope has gone into the past tense lately, we had hoped, I used to think, and picture yourself falling into step beside them.

You don't need the right words: the stranger started with a question and let them talk, so think of one question you could ask, and then just listen. If you pray, you can ask to be good company on someone's road.

wordCard.voice: Emmaus. The village seven miles off, where two sad friends finally recognized Jesus in the breaking of the bread.

orig.note: Greek: the breaking of the bread. Acts uses the same phrase for what the first believers did together.

carryVoice: Your line: was not our heart burning. They knew him in the breaking of bread. Day sixty-nine, done.
